lesson.title: Counting by Ratios: What Coefficients Really Mean
lesson.summary: The coefficients in a balanced equation are exact mole-to-mole ratios, a numeric recipe that tells you precisely how much of each substance reacts or forms relative to the others.
lesson.body:
Once an equation has been balanced, as you learned to do in Balancing Equations, its coefficients stop being just a bookkeeping trick for satisfying conservation of mass and start being genuinely useful information. Each coefficient tells you the relative number of moles, or equivalently the relative number of particles, of that substance involved in the reaction, compared to every other substance in the same equation. A balanced equation is, in effect, a recipe: it does not just say what ingredients are needed, it says in exactly what proportion.

It is worth being precise about the difference between a coefficient and a subscript, since the two numbers sit right next to each other in a formula like 2 H2O but mean completely different things. A subscript, like the 2 in H2O, is baked into the formula itself and tells you how many atoms of that element are inside one molecule of the compound; changing it creates a different substance entirely. A coefficient, like the 2 written in front of H2O, multiplies the entire formula and tells you how many molecules, or moles, of that already-fixed compound are present; changing it just changes the amount, not the identity, of what you have. When no coefficient is written in front of a formula, a coefficient of 1 is implied, exactly the same convention used with the number 1 in ordinary arithmetic.

Because coefficients express a fixed ratio, you can scale a balanced equation up or down and the ratio still holds, whether you are talking about individual molecules, dozens, or moles. Take the balanced iron oxidation equation from the last chapter, 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3. Read directly from the coefficients, this equation says that 4 units of Fe react with 3 units of O2 to produce 2 units of Fe2O3, in that fixed 4-to-3-to-2 ratio, no matter how large the actual reaction is.

Here is a worked numeric example putting that ratio to use. Suppose you have 8 mol of iron and want to know how much oxygen gas is needed to react with all of it, and how much iron(III) oxide will form. The balanced equation gives the ratio of O2 to Fe as 3 to 4, so the moles of O2 needed are 8 mol Fe times (3 mol O2 / 4 mol Fe) = 8 times 3 divided by 4 = 24 divided by 4 = 6 mol O2. Similarly, the ratio of Fe2O3 to Fe is 2 to 4, so the moles of product formed are 8 mol Fe times (2 mol Fe2O3 / 4 mol Fe) = 8 times 2 divided by 4 = 16 divided by 4 = 4 mol Fe2O3. So 8 mol of iron requires 6 mol of oxygen gas and produces 4 mol of iron(III) oxide, and you can sanity-check this against the original 4:3:2 ratio, since 8:6:4 simplifies back down to exactly 4:3:2.

This kind of ratio reasoning, converting moles of one substance into moles of another using coefficients as a conversion factor, is the seed of a much larger topic called stoichiometry, which you will develop further later on. For now, the key habit to build is this: whenever you see a balanced equation, read its coefficients not as decoration but as a precise numeric recipe you can scale to any quantity you need.
